action.text: Move out of direct sun immediately, apply cool damp clean cloths gently to tender skin, wear loose soft sun-blocking fabric over the area, and rehydrate steadily with safe potable water.
Leave intact sunburn blisters unbroken and avoid petroleum jelly, butter, or topical benzocaine/home remedies that trap heat or trigger allergic skin reactions.
Escalate to prompt clinical evaluation for widespread blistering, severe facial swelling, fever, chills, nausea, confusion, or signs of blister infection (pus, spreading red streaks).

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Protect sun-damaged skin from infection and recognize systemic sunburn illness requiring medical care.
applies: Extended high-UV outdoor exposure on water, alpine snow, or open trails leading to painful red or blistering sunburn.
equipment: Shade cover, cool damp cloths, safe drinking water, loose breathable clothing, and clean sterile dressings for broken blisters.

failure.text: Continuing full-sun paddling with raw blistering shoulders until fever, dehydration, and secondary skin infection develop.

verify.text: Confirm UV exposure is blocked, hydration is maintained, intact blisters are protected, and systemic fever/chills are absent.

stop.text: Extensive blistering, fever/chills, dizziness, or signs of heat exhaustion/stroke require stopping travel and seeking clinical care.

diagram: Move to shade & cool damp cloth | Hydrate steadily; keep blisters intact | Fever, wide blisters or chills -> MD
visual: Failure-mode diagram connecting unprotected water/snow UV glare through painful blistering and dehydration to shade, cool compresses, and clinical triggers. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Halt ascent immediately at early Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS) cues
origin: CDC Travel to High Altitudes; new manuscript

action.text: Suspect Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS) whenever a recently ascended traveler develops headache plus nausea, loss of appetite, unusual fatigue, dizziness, or poor sleep—remembering fitness does NOT protect against altitude illness.
Stop ascending IMMEDIATELY—never climb higher to sleep with AMS symptoms; rest at the current elevation, stay hydrated and warm, avoid alcohol/sedatives, and monitor closely with a companion.
Descend promptly to a lower elevation if symptoms fail to improve after rest or worsen in any way, rather than pushing over a high pass.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent mild altitude headache from progressing into fatal high-altitude lung or brain swelling.
applies: Mountain travel above roughly 8,000 feet (2,500 meters), regardless of athletic fitness.
equipment: Elevation map, written symptom tracker, shelter/warmth, safe hydration, and pre-planned lower-elevation descent route.

failure.text: Calling a throbbing high-altitude headache and vomiting "normal trail fatigue" and hiking 2,000 feet higher to camp.

verify.text: Confirm ascent halted immediately, buddy monitoring is continuous, and a safe lower-elevation descent path is identified.

stop.text: Any worsening headache, repeated vomiting, shortness of breath at rest, or stumbling balance transitions immediately to emergency HAPE/HACE descent.

diagram: >8,000 ft + headache/nausea/fatigue | Halt ascent immediately; never climb higher | Worsening cues -> descend & evacuate
visual: Three-tier altitude-illness escalation ladder separating early AMS halt-ascent from progressive worsening descent and HAPE/HACE life-threat evacuation. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Execute assisted descent and rescue for life-threatening HAPE and HACE
origin: CDC Travel to High Altitudes; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize HAPE (shortness of breath while resting, dry or pink frothy cough, chest tightness, extreme fatigue, bluish lips) and HACE (ataxia/staggering walk as if intoxicated, confusion, slurred speech, severe lethargy)—both are rapidly fatal without descent and medical care.

Activate emergency rescue immediately AND organize assisted descent to substantially lower elevation as soon as terrain, weather, and party safety permit—NEVER let an impaired HAPE/HACE patient descend alone or wait until morning if safe assisted descent is feasible.

Keep the patient warm, minimize their physical exertion (carry their pack, support balance closely, or await SAR evacuation if steep/night terrain makes moving unsafe), and leave prescription altitude medications strictly to clinicians or the patient's own prescribed regimen.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize fatal high-altitude pulmonary or cerebral edema and organize immediate assisted descent and emergency care.
applies: Mountain travel at high elevation when a person develops resting breathlessness, persistent cough, staggering balance, or confusion.
equipment: Emergency comms/SAR activation, warm layers, headlamps, and group support for safe assisted descent.

failure.text: Leaving a confused, staggering hiker alone in a high-camp tent overnight hoping symptoms will clear by sunrise.

verify.text: Confirm emergency rescue is notified, patient is never left alone, exertion is minimized, and safe assisted descent or SAR extraction is underway.

stop.text: Any ataxia, confusion, resting breathlessness, or pink frothy cough is an absolute life-threatening emergency demanding descent and clinical care.

diagram: Resting breathlessness or staggering | Never leave alone; minimize exertion | Assisted safe descent + urgent 911/SAR
visual: Decision tree pairing HAPE/HACE red flags with terrain/weather safety gates to execute assisted descent or urgent SAR extraction. Conceptual, not to scale.
reviewer: Mountain medicine and search and rescue

title: Recognize ongoing lightning hazards and coordinate emergency care
origin: NWS Lightning Tips and American Red Cross; new manuscript

action.text: Check ongoing lightning, terrain and electrical hazards before approaching. A lightning victim does not retain an electrical charge, but the site may still be dangerous.
With multiple casualties, tell 911 which people are unresponsive and not breathing normally. Begin resuscitation when safe and follow dispatch on priorities.

Activate 911 immediately, start trained/dispatcher-guided CPR and AED use on anyone not breathing normally, and arrange clinical evaluation for ALL struck persons (checking burns, hearing/eye injury, and spinal precautions).

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Provide safe immediate resuscitation after a lightning strike without exposing rescuers to ongoing storm danger.
applies: Outdoor group struck by direct lightning or ground current during a thunderstorm.
equipment: Phone/radio for 911, AED if near a building, and ground insulation once scene is clear.

failure.text: Avoiding touching a struck teammate out of fear of leftover electricity, or tending a conscious bruised hiker first while a non-breathing victim goes without CPR.

verify.text: Confirm scene safety, immediate 911/CPR for non-breathing victims first, and medical referral for every affected party member.

stop.text: If ongoing lightning makes care unsafe, tell dispatch and follow its direction on movement and resuscitation.

diagram: Check continuing strike risk | Tell 911 casualty count and breathing | Start safe dispatcher-guided care
visual: Rescue sequence separating the scene hazard from the electrical state of the patient.
reviewer: Emergency medicine, lightning safety, and EMS

title: Recognize anaphylaxis and assist with a patient's prescribed epinephrine
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Anaphylaxis; new manuscript

action.text: Suspect anaphylaxis when airway symptoms, breathing difficulty, faintness, or symptoms across more than one body system develop after a likely allergen. A severe reaction can occur without hives.
Call 911 and assist promptly with the patient’s prescribed epinephrine auto-injector as directed by its instructions and their action plan. Record when it was used.
Do not wait for antihistamines. Avoid having the patient stand or walk. Follow dispatcher directions about positioning and monitor breathing.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Spot rapidly fatal multi-system allergic reactions and support timely use of the patient's own prescribed auto-injector plus 911 activation.
applies: Sudden severe allergic reaction to stings, foods, medications, or latex causing hives plus breathing, throat, stomach, or blood-pressure signs.
equipment: Patient's own prescribed unexpired epinephrine auto-injector (if carried), watch, and 911 communication.

failure.text: Giving an over-the-counter antihistamine and waiting thirty minutes while throat swelling progresses to complete airway closure.

verify.text: Confirm 911 is dispatched, exact auto-injector time is recorded, and breathing/alertness are tracked continuously.

stop.text: If symptoms persist or return, tell 911 immediately. Follow the action plan, product directions and dispatcher advice about a second device.

diagram: Recognize a serious allergic reaction | Call 911 and help use prescribed device | Monitor for persistent or returning symptoms
visual: Three-tier anaphylaxis escalation ladder contrasting mild localized itching from systemic anaphylaxis own-epinephrine assistance and urgent hospital care. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Guard against rebound (biphasic) anaphylaxis after initial improvement
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Anaphylaxis; new manuscript

action.text: Understand that anaphylaxis can rebound hours later ("biphasic reaction") with renewed airway swelling and shock even after initial epinephrine completely resolves hives and wheezing.

Cancel the remainder of the outing immediately and transport or evacuate the patient to an emergency department for clinical observation and follow-up care—never resume remote backcountry travel after an anaphylactic event.
Keep the patient resting calmly with continuous buddy monitoring during exit, keeping their spare prescribed auto-injector immediately accessible rather than buried in a pack.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Ensure every person treated for anaphylaxis reaches hospital observation even when symptoms seem to vanish completely.
applies: Any patient who experienced systemic allergic symptoms or used a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector outdoors.
equipment: Written timeline log, remaining prescribed spare auto-injector if carried, shelter, and evacuation transport.

failure.text: Continuing deeper into the wilderness after a bee-sting auto-injector clears throat tightness, then experiencing a fatal rebound six hours later without backup doses.

verify.text: Confirm exact trigger, dose time, symptom resolution timeline, and direct evacuation route to a hospital are active.

stop.text: Any returning throat tightness, hives, wheezing, or lightheadedness during evacuation triggers immediate 911 update and follow-up per prescribed device/dispatcher guidance.

diagram: Initial relief does NOT end risk | Biphasic rebound can strike hours later | Abort trip; mandatory hospital observation
visual: Time-progression biphasic anaphylaxis timeline mapping initial reaction, auto-injector relief, delayed rebound window, and mandatory hospital observation. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Manage routine bee and wasp stings while screening for systemic reactions
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Anaphylaxis and First Aid; new manuscript

action.text: Move promptly away from the nest or swarm zone to prevent multiple stings; if a honeybee stinger remains in skin, scrape it off promptly sideways with a flat edge (card/fingernail) or pull gently without squeezing a visible venom sac.
Wash the sting area gently with soap and safe water, remove rings near finger stings early before swelling builds, and apply a cool clean damp cloth for comfort.

Watch closely for at least 30 to 60 minutes for systemic anaphylaxis signs (hives away from the sting, lip/tongue swelling, wheezing, dizziness, vomiting), stings inside the mouth/throat, or heavy multiple-sting swarms—all require immediate 911 activation.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Relieve localized insect stings cleanly and distinguish normal local swelling from life-threatening allergic or multiple-sting emergencies.
applies: Honeybee, yellowjacket, hornet, or wasp stings outdoors.
equipment: Flat stiff card edge, soap and safe water, cool compress, and watch.

failure.text: Dismissing spreading hives on the chest and hoarse voice after a hand sting as a "normal strong reaction."

verify.text: Confirm stinger removed, rings off, local site cleaned, and zero distant hives or breathing symptoms over monitoring window.

stop.text: Any throat/mouth sting, breathing change, dizziness, widespread hives, or dozens of stings escalates immediately to 911.

diagram: Leave nest & scrape stinger promptly | Wash clean, remove rings & cool cloth | Distant hives/breath/mouth sting -> 911
visual: Decision tree separating localized sting cleaning/cooling from mouth/throat, multi-sting, and systemic anaphylaxis 911 activation. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Perform daily tick checks, vertical fine-tipped removal, and rash watch
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Tick Bites; new manuscript

action.text: Conduct thorough head-to-toe tick checks at the end of every outdoor day (checking scalp, behind ears, armpits, waistband, groin, and behind knees) and shower promptly after returning home.

Grasp an attached tick as close to the skin surface as possible with fine-tipped tweezers and pull straight upward with steady, even pressure—NEVER twist, crush the body, burn with matches, or smother with petroleum jelly/nail polish.

Wash the bite site and hands thoroughly with soap and safe water, note the date and location on your body, and seek medical evaluation promptly if a rash (expanding bull's-eye or other rash), fever, chills, body aches, or joint swelling appears within 30 days.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Remove attached ticks intact early to reduce Upper Midwest tick-borne illness risk and recognize delayed clinical warning signs.
applies: Any travel in wooded, brushy, tall-grass, or deer-habitat areas (including Minnesota spring through autumn).
equipment: Fine-tipped tweezers, soap and safe water or alcohol swab, small magnifying lens if carried, and calendar/symptom log.

failure.text: Covering an attached deer tick with petroleum jelly or touching it with a hot match tip, which irritates the tick and increases pathogen transfer.

verify.text: Confirm tick pulled straight upward cleanly, site washed, and bite date logged for 30-day symptom watch.

stop.text: Any expanding rash, unexplained fever, severe headache, facial droop, or joint pain within weeks of tick exposure requires prompt clinical evaluation.

diagram: Daily full-body check in brush zones | Fine tweezers close to skin; pull straight | Wash clean & watch rash/fever 30 days
visual: Correct versus incorrect tick removal contrasting fine-tipped straight-up skin-level pull against burning, smothering, or twisting. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Clean mammal bites thoroughly and arrange prompt infection and rabies review
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Animal Bites; new manuscript

action.text: Move safely away from the animal (do NOT try to trap or touch a wild or aggressive animal), then wash the bite immediately and thoroughly with soap and copious running potable water for several minutes to flush saliva and bacteria out.

Control active bleeding with clean direct pressure, cover loosely with a sterile dressing without sealing dirty puncture wounds shut with glue, and document animal species, behavior, and location (or owner vaccination contact if domestic).

Obtain prompt medical evaluation for EVERY skin-breaking mammal bite—clinicians assess infection risk (especially deep cat/hand bites), tetanus currency, and urgent rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent severe bite-wound infection, tetanus, and fatal rabies through immediate washing and mandatory clinical consultation.
applies: Any wild or domestic mammal bite or deep scratch breaking skin (dog, raccoon, skunk, fox, squirrel, coyote, stray cat).
equipment: Soap, copious clean running potable water, clean sterile dressing, and public-health/medical contact.

failure.text: Washing a raccoon scratch lightly with a wet wipe and skipping medical follow-up because the scratch looks small.

verify.text: Confirm prolonged soap-and-potable-water wash completed, bleeding controlled, animal details noted, and clinical evaluation scheduled promptly.

stop.text: Deep bleeding bites, bites to face/hands/joints, or contact with wild rabies-vector species require immediate same-day emergency medical care.

diagram: Scene safe; never capture wild animal | Wash deeply with soap & running water | Same-day clinical infection & rabies review
visual: Four-step mammal-bite care plate mapping scene safety, thorough soap-and-water flush, clean loose cover, and clinical tetanus/rabies evaluation. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Treat indoor bat encounters as potential rabies exposures requiring public-health review
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Animal Bites; new manuscript

action.text: Understand that rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms begin, yet completely preventable with timely clinical post-exposure treatment—and tiny bat bites often leave NO visible mark or wake a sleeping person.

If a bat is found in a room with a sleeping person, unattended child, or anyone who cannot reliably rule out contact—or if any direct skin contact occurs—wash any contact site with soap and water and contact your local health department or doctor promptly.

Never handle a bat with bare hands; if public health advises safe capture for testing, avoid crushing the head and do not risk being bitten—if the bat flies away or cannot be tested, clinical rabies risk assessment still applies immediately.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize that bat teeth can leave invisible painless bites during sleep and trigger timely public-health rabies assessment.
applies: Finding a bat inside a cabin, tent, or bedroom with a sleeping person, young child, intoxicated person, or anyone unable to confirm zero contact.
equipment: Local public-health/clinic phone contact and thick leather gloves ONLY if safe containment is directed by health authorities.

failure.text: Shooing a bat out of a cabin bedroom where children were sleeping and assuming "nobody saw a bite, so no doctor is needed."

verify.text: Confirm zero bare-hand contact occurred and medical/public-health consultation is initiated promptly for any uncertain sleeping-room exposure.

stop.text: Any confirmed bat bite/scratch or uncertain exposure during sleep requires prompt clinical consultation—never wait for symptoms.

diagram: Bat bites can be invisible & painless | Never touch bats with bare hands | Uncertain sleep exposure -> public health MD
visual: Decision tree evaluating confirmed contact, sleeping-room exposure, and bare-hand avoidance to trigger prompt public-health rabies review. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Manage suspected venomous snakebites calmly while rejecting harmful folklore
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Bites and First Aid; new manuscript

action.text: Move out of striking range, call 911 and keep the bitten person at rest. A photograph is optional only from a safe distance and without delaying care. Never try to catch or handle the snake.

Remove rings, watches, bracelets, and tight clothing near the bitten limb immediately before rapid swelling begins, keep the limb comfortably supported at roughly heart level (or per dispatcher/toxicology guidance), and mark the leading edge of swelling with time.

NEVER cut the bite wound, suck venom by mouth or suction kit, apply ice/cold packs, wrap a tourniquet or tight constricting band, or apply electric shocks—all worsen tissue loss and delay hospital antivenom.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Slow systemic venom spread through calm immobilization and rapid hospital transport while preventing tissue destruction from obsolete folklore.
applies: Suspected venomous snakebite (e.g., rattlesnake, copperhead, cottonmouth) during outdoor travel.
equipment: Watch, pen to mark swelling border/time, splint/sling for calm rest, and emergency communications.

failure.text: Cutting X-marks over fang punctures and tying a tight belt above the ankle while hiking rapidly back to the trailhead.

verify.text: Confirm rings/tight items removed, patient resting calm and still, swelling edge marked with time, and urgent hospital transport active.

stop.text: Every suspected venomous snakebite requires emergency hospital evaluation and observation—even if initial pain seems mild ("dry bites" still need clinical monitoring).

title: Evaluate spider bites and scorpion stings with Poison Control guidance
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Spider Bites and Poison Control; new manuscript

action.text: Wash the bite site gently with soap and safe water, apply a clean cool damp cloth (not bare ice) for local discomfort, elevate the limb if comfortable, and keep the person resting calmly.

Call 911 immediately for breathing difficulty, throat/facial swelling, severe chest/abdominal muscle cramping, uncontrollable pain, confusion, or young children/older adults showing systemic symptoms.

For evolving local pain, muscle spasms, blistering/darkening ulcers, or uncertain species exposure, contact Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) or seek clinical evaluation without applying improvised poultices or cutting the skin.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Separate minor arthropod bites from systemic neurotoxic or necrotic envenomations requiring Poison Control or EMS care.
applies: Suspected black widow, brown recluse, or scorpion stings/bites causing escalating pain, cramps, or systemic illness.
equipment: Soap and safe water, cool compress, Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in U.S.) or 911 access, and safe photo if already dead.

failure.text: Ignoring severe abdominal rigidity and sweating after a widow spider bite or attempting home incision of a blistered bite wound.

verify.text: Confirm site washed cleanly, symptom progression timed, and Poison Control or EMS contacted for any systemic or worsening local signs.

stop.text: Severe muscle cramps, trouble breathing, spreading blistering/ulceration, or pediatric systemic symptoms mandate urgent hospital care.

diagram: Clean site & cool damp cloth | Call Poison Control for evolving bites | Cramps, breath labor or child -> 911
visual: Three-tier arthropod-bite escalation ladder separating clean local care from Poison Control consultation and urgent 911 systemic emergency. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Separate 911 emergencies from Poison Control calls after toxic ingestions
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Poisoning and Poison Control; new manuscript

action.text: Call 911 IMMEDIATELY if the person is unresponsive, drowsy, seizing, struggling to breathe, or having chest pain; if the person is awake and alert with no immediate life threat, call U.S. Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) immediately for specialist guidance.

Call U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for case-specific advice if the person is stable. Read the label or use a photo already taken safely. Do not gather or transport an unknown substance if that risks exposure.

NEVER induce vomiting, give syrup of ipecac, force milk/saltwater, or administer improvised camp charcoal unless explicitly directed by Poison Control or an emergency clinician—vomiting caustics or fuels burns airways and lungs severely.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Deliver exact substance details to toxicology specialists rapidly while preventing dangerous improvised vomiting or home antidotes.
applies: Accidental swallowing, inhalation, or skin exposure to unknown wild plants, mushrooms, camp fuel, water chemicals, or household toxins.
equipment: Container/label or safely bagged plant/mushroom specimen (no bare-hand contamination), watch, and phone access.

failure.text: Forcing a child who sipped stove fuel to vomit, driving hydrocarbons directly into the lungs and causing severe chemical pneumonia.

verify.text: Confirm exact substance/container saved, exposure time noted, zero unguided vomiting induced, and 911 or Poison Control engaged.

stop.text: In remote areas without phone access, evacuate immediately to clinical care after any unknown toxic plant, mushroom, fuel, or chemical ingestion.

diagram: Unresponsive/seizing/breath -> 911 | Awake/alert -> Poison Control + label | Never induce vomiting or DIY charcoal
visual: Decision tree separating immediate 911 life-threat activation from Poison Control specialist consultation and remote evacuation with saved specimen/label. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Wash urushiol oils promptly and avoid deadly poison-ivy smoke inhalation
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Wounds and Poisoning; new manuscript

action.text: If exposed to suspected poison ivy, oak, or sumac, rinse skin thoroughly as soon as possible with COOL running water and mild soap (avoiding hot water initially, and scrubbing gently under fingernails) to wash away sticky urushiol oil before it binds.

Isolate and wash contaminated clothing, shoelaces, tools, and pet fur carefully—urushiol oil remains active on fabric and gear for months and spreads easily to faces and eyes, whereas rash blister fluid itself does NOT spread the rash.
NEVER burn poison ivy, oak, or sumac brush in campfires or yard piles—inhaling urushiol smoke causes severe, life-threatening airway and lung swelling requiring immediate 911 emergency care.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Limit contact dermatitis from poison ivy, oak, or sumac through fast cold-water washing and prevent severe lung injury from burning vines.
applies: Wooded, shoreline, and trailside brush in Upper Midwest and North American habitats.
equipment: Cool safe water, mild soap, clean spare clothing, and sealed bag for contaminated garments/boots.

failure.text: Tossing dead hairy poison-ivy vines onto a campfire and inhaling toxic smoke, or wiping unwashed oily hands across the eyes.

verify.text: Confirm exposed skin, fingernails, and tools were washed thoroughly with cool soap/water and zero vines enter any fire.

stop.text: Any facial/eye swelling, widespread blistering, breathing difficulty after smoke exposure, or signs of secondary skin infection require prompt clinical care.

diagram: Wash skin/nails fast with cool soap | Isolate oily clothes, boots & pet fur | NEVER burn vines; smoke -> urgent 911

title: Manage dehydration, diarrhea, and vomiting with small-sip oral rehydration
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Dehydration and CDC Safe Water; new manuscript

action.text: For alert patients able to swallow, offer frequent tiny sips (a spoonful or small sip every few minutes) of confirmed potable water or commercial labeled oral rehydration solution—gulping large volumes rapidly often triggers renewed vomiting.
Enforce strict caregiver and patient handwashing with soap and safe water plus isolated waste containment to stop fecal-oral gastrointestinal illness from disabling the entire group.

Evacuate promptly for medical care if vomiting prevents keeping fluids down over hours, stools contain blood or black tar, high fever develops, urine stops or turns very dark, or dizziness/confusion appear.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Maintain safe hydration during gastrointestinal illness or heat loss and catch severe dehydration red flags before collapse.
applies: Traveler's diarrhea, vomiting, heat exertion, or inadequate drinking-water intake during backcountry or outage events.
equipment: Confirmed potable drinking water, labeled commercial oral rehydration salts (ORS) if carried, clean cup, and strict hand hygiene.

failure.text: Drinking large cold gulps rapidly while nauseated (worsening vomiting) or ignoring zero urination and confusion in a child or older adult.

verify.text: Confirm fluids are confirmed potable, sips stay down steadily, urine output/color is tracked, and hand hygiene isolates the group.

stop.text: Inability to hold fluids down, bloody diarrhea, sunken eyes, fainting, or altered mental status require urgent clinical IV rehydration.

visual: Four-step dehydration management plate showing potable water verification, small-sip pacing, group sanitation isolation, and clinical evacuation red flags. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Support companions with known asthma, diabetes, or heart conditions outdoors
origin: NIH MedlinePlus First Aid and FEMA Access Needs; new manuscript

action.text: Before departure, ask willing companions privately to share critical emergency needs (asthma inhaler location, epinephrine location, diabetes fast-acting glucose, seizure plan, or cardiac medications) and keep a written summary accessible.

During a flare-up, stop exertion immediately, provide calm shelter, and assist ONLY with the person's OWN prescribed labeled rescue device or documented personal action plan—never adjust prescription dosages or share another person's medication.

Activate 911/EMS early whenever a chronic condition fails to respond promptly to the person's own rescue plan, requires repeated rescue doses, or causes breathing distress, chest pain, or altered alertness.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Plan ahead for known chronic medical needs so companions can assist with a person's own prescribed emergency tools safely.
applies: Trips and households including individuals with asthma, severe allergies, diabetes, seizure disorders, or cardiac history.
equipment: Written personal emergency action plan, patient's own labeled prescribed rescue devices, and accessible backup supplies.

failure.text: Discovering mid-trip that a companion's rescue inhaler or epinephrine is buried at the bottom of a locked car at the trailhead.

verify.text: Confirm personal rescue devices are carried on the person (protected from freezing/heat) and trip leaders know where they are stored.

stop.text: Unrelieved breathing distress, chest pain, persistent confusion, or exhausted rescue supplies require immediate trip abort and 911 activation.

title: Protect a person during a seizure without restraining limbs or entering the mouth
origin: American Red Cross and NIH MedlinePlus First Aid; new manuscript

action.text: Time the seizure and move hazards away if safe. Protect the head with something soft.
Do not hold the person down or place anything in their mouth.

Check breathing and use a safe side position when appropriate. Call 911 if it lasts longer than five minutes, repeats without recovery, happens in water, or causes injury, breathing or waking difficulty. Follow CDC or dispatcher directions for pregnancy, diabetes or a first seizure.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent head and airway injury during a convulsive seizure while knowing exact timing and 911 activation triggers.
applies: Witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure outdoors or during an emergency.
equipment: Soft jacket/pad for head cushioning, watch to time seizure duration, and 911 access.

failure.text: Trying to pry open a seizing person's jaw with a stick or failing to time the seizure duration for arriving EMS.

verify.text: Confirm exact seizure duration recorded, surroundings cleared, post-seizure side-lying airway check performed, and 911 rules applied.

stop.text: If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, activate 911 and start dispatcher-guided CPR.

title: Distinguish alert low blood sugar from unresponsive diabetic emergencies
origin: NIH MedlinePlus First Aid and American Red Cross; new manuscript

action.text: Watch for rapid low-blood-sugar (hypoglycemia) onset during heavy outdoor exertion or skipped meals—sweating, trembling, sudden weakness, irritability, or dizziness—and stop activity immediately.
If the person is fully awake and can swallow safely, assist with their own rapid glucose plan. Follow the plan and check whether symptoms resolve.
For impaired alertness, seizure or inability to swallow, give nothing by mouth. Call 911 promptly and follow the patient’s emergency plan and dispatcher.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Support safe fast-acting sugar only when a diabetic patient is fully able to swallow, and call 911 immediately if altered or unresponsive.
applies: Known person with diabetes developing sudden shakiness, sweating, pale skin, irritability, confusion, or collapse during physical exertion or delayed meals.
equipment: Patient's own glucose tablets/gel/juice, personal diabetes action plan, and 911 communication.

failure.text: Pouring fruit juice into the mouth of a drowsy, slurring diabetic hiker who cannot protect their airway.

verify.text: Confirm the patient is alert and swallowing safely before giving anything by mouth. Monitor for deterioration.

stop.text: Declining alertness, inability to swallow or unresponsiveness requires emergency help immediately.

diagram: Awake and swallowing: own action plan | Impaired alertness: nothing by mouth | Call 911 for severe signs
visual: Branch decision tree splitting alert safe-swallowing fast sugar from altered/unresponsive zero-oral-intake 911 emergency care. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Protect children and older adults against rapid exposure and shock decline
origin: CDC Cold/Heat Health and NIH MedlinePlus Dehydration; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize that infants and young children lose body heat much faster (high surface-area-to-mass ratio), dehydrate rapidly during vomiting/diarrhea, and deteriorate abruptly from shock or heat illness after looking "fine" minutes earlier.

Monitor older adults closely for blunted thirst/cold sensation, balance/fall hazards, blood-thinner bleeding risks (minor head bumps can cause serious delayed bleeding), and heat-wave medication sensitivity.

Lower your stop-and-evacuate threshold dramatically for children and older adults—turn back early, insulate proactively before shivering starts, and contact EMS/clinicians promptly rather than watching and waiting overnight.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Adjust prevention, pacing, and evacuation thresholds early for vulnerable age groups with smaller physiological reserves.
applies: Families, youth groups, and older companions exposed to cold, heat, dehydration, altitude, or trauma.
equipment: Extra insulating layers, shade, frequent hydration/snack reminders, written medical/allergy cards, and conservative turnaround times.

failure.text: Expecting a small child or frail older adult to maintain adult pacing in cold rain or high heat until sudden lethargy or collapse occurs.

verify.text: Confirm extra warmth/water checks are scheduled frequently and any head bump on blood thinners or pediatric lethargy triggers prompt medical review.

stop.text: Unusual quietness/lethargy in a child, minimal wet diapers/urine, or ANY head injury in an older adult taking anticoagulants mandates prompt clinical evaluation.

diagram: Kids/elders lose heat & fluids faster | Lower turn-back & shelter thresholds | Early clinical review; blood thinners flag
visual: Comparative configuration contrasting pediatric rapid heat/fluid loss, older-adult medication/fall flags, and conservative group turnaround gates. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Stabilize acute panic and psychological shock during delayed rescue
origin: NPS Emergency Plan and American Red Cross; new manuscript

action.text: Check for physical causes of agitation FIRST (low oxygen, head injury, shock, low blood sugar, hypothermia, or heat stroke)—never label sudden confusion or combativeness "just panic" before ruling out medical red flags.

Once physical life threats are addressed, speak calmly in short concrete sentences, shelter the person from wind/noise, guide slow steady breathing (in slowly through the nose, long calm exhale), and give simple grounding tasks (holding a pad, checking a watch).
Keep distressed companions paired with a calm buddy at all times so fear never drives impulsive solo flight into dark, cold, or hazardous terrain.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Calm acute distress and prevent panic-driven wandering or hyperventilation while preserving group decision quality.
applies: Lost parties, storm-trapped groups, trauma witnesses, or injured companions awaiting delayed rescue.
equipment: Calm clear voice, shelter/warmth, simple structured tasks, and buddy pairing.

failure.text: Calling a hypothermic or head-injured hiker's agitation "hysteria" and missing life-threatening physiological decline, or letting a panicked person bolt down trail alone.

verify.text: Confirm medical causes of confusion were screened first, calm breathing/shelter is active, and continuous buddy supervision prevents wandering.

stop.text: Persistent confusion, inability to stay safely with the group, or self-harm risk requires priority assisted evacuation and clinical/crisis support.

diagram: Screen physical red flags FIRST | Shelter, slow breath & clear short cues | Buddy-pair always; block impulsive flight
visual: Decision tree screening physiological hypoxia/shock/cold/head-injury causes first before applying calm grounding and buddy-pairing support. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Handle knocked-out teeth and facial dental emergencies conservatively
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Wounds and First Aid; new manuscript

action.text: For a knocked-out permanent adult tooth, pick it up ONLY by the white biting crown—NEVER touch or scrub the delicate root—rinse briefly with clean water/saline ONLY if dirty, and store submerged in cold milk or sterile saline (do NOT store dry or scrub) while heading immediately to a dentist/ED.
Control gum socket bleeding by having an alert patient bite firmly on clean folded damp gauze, and save any broken tooth fragments cleanly without gluing anything back in the mouth.

Treat toothache accompanied by expanding cheek/jaw/neck swelling, fever, difficulty swallowing, or eye-area swelling as an urgent spreading deep-infection emergency requiring immediate clinical care (never wait days in camp).

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Preserve a knocked-out permanent tooth cleanly for rapid dental re-implantation while spotting dangerous facial infection swelling.
applies: Falls, paddle strikes, or biting hard food causing tooth avulsion, broken teeth, or sudden severe toothache with jaw/cheek swelling.
equipment: Clean gauze, small clean container with milk/saline (or patient's own saliva if alert), and urgent dental/clinical contact.

failure.text: Scrubbing the root of a knocked-out permanent tooth with soap and wrapping it dry in tissue paper, or ignoring jaw swelling and fever that threaten the airway.

verify.text: Confirm tooth handled by crown only in moist milk/saline, bleeding controlled with gauze, and any facial swelling/fever triggers urgent exit.

stop.text: Spreading facial/neck swelling, fever, trouble swallowing/breathing, or severe uncontrolled oral bleeding requires immediate 911/emergency department care.

title: Respect lay limits for ear pain, ear/nose foreign objects, and barotrauma
origin: NIH MedlinePlus First Aid and Wounds; new manuscript

action.text: NEVER insert tweezers, sticks, cotton swabs, or improvised probes deep into an ear canal or nostril to dig out a foreign object—blind probing commonly ruptures eardrums or pushes objects deeper into the airway.

For painful elevation-change ear pressure (barotrauma), slow descent/ascent, yawn, or swallow gently—never force hard blowing if severe sharp pain occurs; do NOT put random liquids or oils into an ear that has fluid, blood, or suspected eardrum rupture.

Seek prompt clinical evaluation for any embedded ear/nose object, blood or clear fluid draining from an ear after head trauma (immediate 911 red flag), severe worsening ear pain with fever, or sudden hearing loss/vertigo.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Avoid rupturing eardrums or pushing foreign objects deeper while recognizing inner-ear and sinus red flags.
applies: Insects or seeds in ears/noses, elevation-descent ear pressure, or severe ear pain/drainage outdoors.
equipment: Calm light inspection only (no deep probing) and clinical referral plan.

failure.text: Digging at a pebble or tick inside a child's ear canal with pocketknife tweezers, tearing the eardrum.

verify.text: Confirm zero deep probing occurred, no unapproved drops entered a draining ear, and head-trauma ear drainage triggers immediate 911.

stop.text: Clear/bloody ear drainage after head injury, severe vertigo, facial weakness, or high fever with ear swelling requires urgent emergency care.

diagram: Zero deep probes into ear or nose | Never pour drops in draining/injured ear | Head-trauma drainage -> immediate 911
visual: System boundary diagram contrasting safe external observation and clinical removal against hazardous deep probing and unapproved ear drops. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Act immediately on carbon monoxide poisoning cues with fresh air and 911
origin: CPSC Carbon Monoxide Fact Sheet and CDC CO Basics; new manuscript

action.text: Suspect carbon monoxide immediately when one or more people in an enclosed or sheltered space develop sudden headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, confusion, weakness, or unexplained drowsiness—especially when multiple companions feel "flu-like" at the same time.

Move EVERY person immediately into clean open outdoor air without stopping to pack gear, keep bystanders out of the contaminated space, and call 911 from outside—remember CO is colorless, odorless, and requires clinical high-flow oxygen evaluation.

Never re-enter a shelter, cabin, or vehicle to retrieve items or silence an alarm before fire/EMS crews meter the air and clear the space; initiate dispatcher-guided CPR outdoors if anyone is unresponsive and not breathing normally.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize silent multi-person CO symptoms indoors, in vehicles, or in tents and evacuate to clean outdoor air immediately.
applies: Any fuel-burning heater, stove, generator, fireplace, or idling vehicle near people in cabins, campers, shelters, or snow-drifted cars.
equipment: Immediate outdoor exit route, working CO alarm (prevention/alert only), and 911 access from outside.

failure.text: Attributing shared tent or cabin headaches and nausea to "bad camp dinner" and going back to sleep while a heater continues running.

verify.text: Confirm all occupants are accounted for in fresh outdoor air, 911 is dispatched, and zero people re-enter until cleared by responders.

stop.text: Any CO alarm, shared headache/nausea near fuel appliances, or collapse near an engine/heater mandates instant outdoor evacuation and 911 care.

diagram: Headache/dizzy/nausea near fuel heat | Exit everyone to fresh air NOW | Call 911 outside; never re-enter
visual: Four-step carbon-monoxide emergency plate showing silent symptom recognition, instant evacuation of all occupants, 911 call from fresh air, and responder air clearance. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Mitigate wildfire smoke and irritant-gas airway exposure outdoors
origin: US EPA AirNow Wildfires and Ready.gov Wildfires; new manuscript

action.text: Move away from dense wildfire smoke plumes promptly, reduce heavy aerobic exertion (which pulls deep PM2.5 particles into lungs), and relocate into an enclosed clean-air indoor room or outside the smoke corridor whenever possible.
A well-fitting particulate respirator can reduce smoke particles. It cannot protect against carbon monoxide, toxic gases or oxygen deficiency. Follow local health alerts and evacuate when directed.

Monitor individuals with asthma, heart disease, pregnancy, children, and older adults closely; assist only with their own prescribed inhalers and call 911 for wheezing, chest pain, persistent coughing, or shortness of breath.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Protect lungs from fine PM2.5 smoke particulates and recognize severe airway distress requiring rapid relocation and clinical care.
applies: Wildland fire smoke plumes, heavy camp smoke inversions, or regional Unhealthy AQI events affecting travelers or households.
equipment: Live AirNow AQI alerts when reachable, properly fitted NIOSH N95/P100 particulate respirator (if essential), and indoor HEPA clean-room access.

failure.text: Running hard trails in Very Unhealthy wildfire smoke wearing a damp bandana under the false belief it blocks fine smoke and gases.

verify.text: Confirm exertion dropped, clean indoor air or route relocation is prioritized, and vulnerable travelers have own inhalers ready.

stop.text: Active advancing flames, thick eye/throat-burning smoke, chest pain, or worsening wheezing requires immediate evacuation and clinical evaluation.

diagram: Reduce exertion & move to clean air | Fitted N95 filters PM2.5 (NOT CO/O2) | Wheezing or chest pain -> urgent 911
visual: Comparative configuration contrasting bandana/surgical mask (no PM2.5 seal), fitted NIOSH N95 (PM2.5 only; no CO/O2), and clean indoor HEPA air/evacuation. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Assemble and inspect a training-matched wilderness first-aid kit
origin: NIH MedlinePlus First Aid and NPS Ten Essentials; new manuscript

action.text: Pack supplies you actually know how to use cleanly under stress—prioritizing scene barriers (nitrile gloves), hemorrhage control (sterile gauze, pressure bandage, plus commercial tourniquet if trained), wound cleaning/dressings, blister padding, tweezers, and a waterproof patient log card.

Omit surgical scalpels, suture kits, unprescribed prescription drugs, or invasive tools you are NOT clinically licensed and trained to use—untrained gear adds weight and tempts dangerous improvisation.

Inspect the entire kit before every season and after every outing to replace used items, verify intact sterile wrappers, discard expired personal medications per instructions, and protect contents in dry waterproof bags.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Carry practical, unexpired, waterproofed first-aid supplies matched strictly to actual caregiver training and route hazards.
applies: Pre-trip kit assembly and seasonal re-inspection for day hikes, backcountry trips, and household go-bags.
equipment: Waterproof labeled pouch, sterile gauze/dressings, tape, nitrile gloves, trauma shears, fine tweezers, blister tape, emergency blanket, written log card/pencil, and personal prescribed items.

failure.text: Carrying a dusty five-year-old kit with dried-out tape, cracked gloves, and complex gadgets no one in the party knows how to operate.

verify.text: Confirm every item is unexpired, dry-packed, familiar to the carrier, and matched to group size and trip length.

stop.text: Do not launch remote multi-day travel with an uninspected kit or missing essential personal rescue medications.

diagram: Match gear strictly to real training | Waterproof barriers, gauze, tweezers, log | Inspect & restock before every trip

title: Protect personal prescription medications from cold, heat, and loss
origin: FEMA Access Needs and NIH MedlinePlus First Aid; new manuscript

action.text: Carry essential personal medications in their original pharmacy-labeled containers (plus an extra multi-day reserve split across a companion's pack if appropriate) so EMS clinicians can verify exact drug names and strengths instantly.

Protect temperature-sensitive prescriptions—epinephrine auto-injectors, insulin, and pressurized asthma inhalers lose potency or malfunction if frozen in winter packs or baked inside parked summer cars; carry them in insulated inner layers close to body warmth in winter or shaded cool pouches in heat.
Keep a waterproof written list of all medications, dosages, prescribing clinics, and allergies inside your wallet and first-aid kit so rescuers have accurate records even if you become unresponsive.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Keep life-sustaining personal prescriptions (epinephrine, insulin, inhalers, heart/seizure meds) potent and accessible in harsh environments.
applies: Any traveler or household member relying on daily or emergency prescription medications outdoors or during outages.
equipment: Original labeled prescription containers, insulated inner-pocket pouch (for cold/heat), written medication/dose/allergy card, and spare supply.

failure.text: Stashing an epinephrine auto-injector or insulin pen in an outer backpack pocket at minus 10°F where the liquid freezes solid before an emergency strikes.

verify.text: Confirm original pharmacy labels, spare backup days, temperature-buffer storage, and written medication/allergy list are packed.

stop.text: Frozen, cloudy/discolored (check drug label), damaged, or expired emergency medications must be replaced before relying on them in remote areas.

diagram: Original pharmacy labels + spare days | Buffer insulin/epi/inhalers from cold/heat | Carry waterproof med & allergy card

title: Understand improvised field-aid boundaries when commercial supplies run short
origin: NIH MedlinePlus First Aid and ACS Stop the Bleed; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize safe lay improvisations when commercial supplies run out: clean folded cloth for direct bleeding pressure, rolled jackets and foam pads for cushioned limb splinting, and dry insulated sleeping bags/tarps for hypothermia wraps.

Recognize hard non-improvisable boundaries: thin shoelaces/cord fail as tourniquets, dirty cloth or untreated water contaminates open wounds, household glues/needles cause deep infection, and improvised pole litters collapse under heavy loads.
Treat ANY improvised stabilization as a temporary bridge strictly meant to keep the patient stable until professional EMS/SAR supplies and clinicians take over.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Know which basic mechanical supports can be improvised safely (clean cloth pressure, padded splints) and which cannot (tourniquets, sterile sutures).
applies: Remote emergencies where commercial first-aid dressings or splints are exhausted or absent.
equipment: Cleanest available dry cloth (bandana, T-shirt), foam sleeping pads, pack stays/clothing for padding, and potable water.

failure.text: Relying on improvised wilderness tricks when carrying basic commercial gauze, nitrile gloves, and a commercial tourniquet (with training) weighs ounces.

verify.text: Confirm cleanest dry cloth used for pressure, generous padding under improvised splints, and zero unsafe improvised closure or thin-cord tourniquets.

stop.text: Whenever improvised stabilization fails to control bleeding, maintain warmth, or protect circulation, escalate urgency with 911/SAR immediately.

diagram: Safe: clean pressure, pad splint, wrap | Unsafe: thin-cord TQ, glue, dirty water | Temporary bridge to EMS only
visual: Correct versus incorrect field improvisation contrasting clean cloth pressure and foam-pad splinting against thin-cord tourniquets and unsterile closure. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Respect remote-setting clinical boundaries: diagnosis, dosing, and invasive care
origin: NIH MedlinePlus First Aid and American Red Cross; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize that lay field exams cannot diagnose internal bleeding, hairline fractures, concussions vs brain bleeds, appendicitis, or cardiac events—use functional red flags (alertness, breathing, bleeding, mobility, trend direction) to drive evacuation decisions instead of guessing diagnoses.

Do NOT prescribe or calculate medication dosages for companions, administer another person's prescription drugs, or perform invasive field procedures (cutting wounds, lancing deep abscesses, field suturing, or airway incisions).

Remember that wilderness first-aid reference cards support memory AFTER hands-on certified training—they NEVER substitute for formal CPR, Stop the Bleed, WFA/WFR courses, or live 911/clinical medical direction.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Maintain disciplined humility about what lay wilderness care can and cannot determine without diagnostics, labs, or clinical licensure.
applies: Every backcountry medical decision across injury, illness, exposure, and evacuation planning.
equipment: Written patient log, communication plan, and pre-agreed conservative evacuation rules.

failure.text: Acting as an amateur physician in camp—guessing a "harmless stomach virus" and withholding evacuation until an appendix ruptures or shock sets in.

verify.text: Confirm decisions rest on objective functional trends and red flags rather than speculative field diagnoses.

stop.text: Uncertainty paired with worsening pain, fever, abnormal breathing, or declining alertness ALWAYS resolves in favor of evacuation and clinical evaluation.

diagram: Track functional trends, not guesses | Zero lay dosing or invasive surgery | Uncertainty + worsening -> evacuate

title: Conduct pre-trip medical screening, group disclosures, and evacuation planning
origin: NPS Hike Smart and FEMA Make a Plan; new manuscript

verify.text: Before departure, list the two most likely route-failure points on today's map and name the exact dry-land bailout for each.

stop.text: When field terrain contradicts the map and no verified detour appears, halt before drifting off-route and reassess from known ground.

title: Execute the lost-in-winter pocket action sequence cleanly
origin: B014-P20 pocket card and NWS winter safety; adapted historical material

action.text: STOP immediately on stable dry land away from ice, wind corridors and overhead snags—sit on pack or foam pad, put on dry insulation and eat/drink safe reserves to protect clear judgment.
THINK and OBSERVE: count the group, screen for early hypothermia (fumbling, slurred speech, confusion), check last confirmed landmark and test whether 911/text/beacon works without risky wandering.
PLAN conservatively: stay put, build a windbreak/dry bed and display high-contrast signals unless an unmistakable, short, verified land route leads to immediate safe shelter.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Follow one clear, cold-stress-proof decision order when disoriented in winter conditions.
applies: Lost, overdue or weather-trapped outdoor party in cold or snowy conditions.
equipment: Dry layers, ground insulation, whistle, light, map and phone/beacon if carried.

failure.text: Panicking and power-walking rapidly in freezing wind to stay warm, sweating out inner layers while moving farther away from the Point Last Seen.

verify.text: Confirm the group is off ice, out of wind, wearing dry insulation, accounted for and either contacting rescue or displaying clear signals.

stop.text: Worsening confusion, slurred speech, frostbite numbness or failing daylight ends all travel options—stabilize in shelter and activate emergency rescue immediately.

diagram: STOP on land & add dry layers | Screen cold signs & call 911 | Stay findable unless exit sure
