title: Prepare for straight-line derechos and damaging hail before outflow gusts hit
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Thunderstorms and NWS; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize that Upper Midwest **derechos** produce sustained straight-line wind gusts rivaling weak-to-moderate tornadoes across hundreds of miles—moving rapidly at 50–70 mph with violent outflow gusts arriving BEFORE rain begins.

Move inside a sturdy building away from windows and skylights immediately upon a Severe Thunderstorm Warning (especially tags noting "Destructive" or 70+ mph winds / large hail)—shut blinds/curtains beforehand to help catch shattering glass and avoid rooms beneath towering dead/leaning yard trees if an interior room exists.
Secure lightweight patio furniture, grills, and loose tools BEFORE storms arrive on Watch days—NEVER run outside during rising outflow gusts to chase trash cans or patio umbrellas.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Treat Severe Thunderstorm Warnings with high-wind/derecho potential seriously to prevent crushing tree falls, glass injuries, and blackouts.
applies: Fast-moving squall lines, bow-echo derechos (70–100+ mph straight-line winds), and severe hailstorms across the Midwest.
equipment: Sturdy indoor interior room away from windows, NOAA/WEA alerts, and pre-storm secured yard furniture.

failure.text: Staying in a glass-walled sunroom or backyard tent during a 85 mph derecho outflow gust that drives hail through panes and drops mature limbs.

verify.text: Confirm household moves inside away from windows/skylights on Severe Thunderstorm Warnings and outdoor gear is secured ahead of storms.

stop.text: Flying debris, shattering glass, or roaring wind shifts require dropping immediately to the lowest interior tornado-safe room.

title: Enforce indoor and outdoor lightning safety plus the 30-minute rule
origin: NWS Lightning Tips and Ready.gov Thunderstorms; new manuscript

action.text: Obey **"When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors"**—lightning strikes 10+ miles away from rain cores under clear blue sky; move immediately inside a substantial enclosed building or hard-topped metal vehicle (windows closed) rather than open picnic pavilions, fabric tents, dugouts, porches, or under trees.

Inside a home during active lightning, stay OFF corded landline phones, avoid touching plugged-in charging electronics, stay away from exterior windows/concrete basement floors/walls (rebar conducts ground current), and do NOT shower, bathe, or wash dishes (plumbing pipes and water conduct lightning current indoors!).
Wait a full **30 MINUTES AFTER THE LAST HEARD THUNDER** before resuming swimming, boating, yard work, or outdoor play—many fatal lightning strikes occur as storms depart.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent direct and conductive indoor/outdoor lightning injuries during every electrical storm.
applies: Homes, yards, lakes, ballfields, and campgrounds whenever thunder is audible or lightning flashes.
equipment: Substantial enclosed building (with wiring/plumbing) or hard-topped metal vehicle with windows rolled up, plus watch for 30-minute timer.

failure.text: Stepping back onto the lake dock five minutes after rain stops while distant thunder still rumbles, or taking a hot shower during a direct thunderstorm.

verify.text: Confirm everyone shelters inside a substantial building/hard-top car at first thunder, avoids indoor plumbing/corded gear, and times a full 30-minute clear window.

stop.text: Any renewed clap of thunder resets the 30-minute indoor safety timer back to zero immediately.

title: Navigate post-tornado and derecho debris safely without secondary injuries
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Tornadoes and Thunderstorms; new manuscript

action.text: Wait until official storm warnings clear before leaving shelter, put on sturdy thick-soled boots and heavy work gloves immediately, and watch every step for shattered glass, upturned nails, splintered lumber, and unstable leaning walls or hanging "widowmaker" tree limbs overhead.

Assume EVERY downed or tangled utility wire is **ENERGIZED AND LETHAL** (stay ≥35+ feet back; never touch wet metal fences, aluminum siding, or tree limbs touching wires), and evacuate immediately if you smell rotten-egg natural gas or hear hissing pipes—using flashlights ONLY, never matches or lighters.

Do NOT enter heavily damaged buildings or crawl into collapsed debris looking for belongings—account for household members/neighbors verbally from safe ground and leave structural search-and-rescue to trained fire/USAR teams.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent electrocution, gas explosions, puncture wounds, and structural collapses during the dangerous hours immediately after windstorms.
applies: Exiting shelters and inspecting damaged neighborhoods after tornadoes, derechos, or severe windstorms.

verify.text: Confirm boots/gloves worn, flashlights only (zero open flames), ≥35 ft clear of downed wires, and damaged buildings left to responders.

title: Recognize why outdoor sirens never replace indoor nighttime warning receivers
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Tornadoes and Alerts; new manuscript

action.text: Understand explicitly that municipal **outdoor warning sirens** are engineered ONLY to alert people who are OUTDOORS—modern double-pane windows, air conditioners, heavy rain, wind roar, and rural distances routinely make sirens completely inaudible inside sleeping bedrooms.

Place a loud battery-backed **NOAA Weather Radio** programmed with your county SAME code inside your bedroom AND verify smartphone **Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA)** remain turned ON and allowed to sound through nighttime Do-Not-Disturb settings.
Keep sturdy shoes, a flashlight, and phone charger beside the bed on evening Tornado Watch nights so waking to an alarm leads straight to basement shelter in seconds.

title: Distinguish slow river/snowmelt floods from sudden Flash Flood Warnings
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Floods and NWS; new manuscript

action.text: Distinguish **river/snowmelt flooding** (builds over hours to days with predictable crest forecasts—allowing early document/vehicle moving, utility prep, and orderly evacuation) from **Flash Flooding** (erupts within minutes from intense rainstorms, clogged urban drains, ice jams, or dam/levee failures with violent wall-of-water surges).

Act IMMEDIATELY on a **Flash Flood Warning** or **Flash Flood Emergency**: move straight to verified higher ground on foot or along open high roads BEFORE low streets, underpasses, and creek bridges vanish underwater.
Remember that levees and dams reduce risk rather than eliminating it—any official levee-breach or dam-failure evacuation order demands instant high-ground departure with zero delay.

title: Obey Turn Around Don't Drown: 6-inch walking and 12-inch vehicle flood physics
origin: NWS Turn Around Don't Drown and Ready.gov Floods; new manuscript

action.text: NWS depth examples illustrate how little moving water can knock people down or sweep away cars. They are warnings, not decision thresholds. Flooded roads can conceal damaged pavement or dangerous current.

NEVER drive around "Road Closed" barricades or into flooded underpasses/roads—especially at night when murky water hides completely washed-out pavement, open storm manholes, and deep sinkholes beneath an apparently shallow surface.
Turn around immediately to an open high-ground detour, OR wait safely on high dry ground until waters recede and highway crews verify bridge/roadbed integrity.

title: Seek safe elevated refuge if sudden flash floodwater traps roads or homes
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Floods; new manuscript

action.text: If floodwater surrounds your home and safe dry evacuation is NO LONGER POSSIBLE, move immediately to the **HIGHEST OPEN LEVEL** of the building—never stay in a basement or crawlspace where rising water and electrical hazards trap people rapidly.

**NEVER climb into a closed, windowless attic** where rising floodwater can trap you beneath a solid roof with no escape—climb onto the roof ONLY if rising water forces you upward as a last resort, call 911 with your exact address, and signal clearly for water/air rescue.
Do NOT enter rushing outdoor floodwater trying to swim or wade to safety—wait for trained swift-water rescue teams unless the structure itself is actively collapsing.

verify.text: Confirm household knows highest open-access refuge level, avoids closed windowless attics, and calls 911 early if surrounded.

title: Avoid flooded roads and call for rescue if trapped in a vehicle
origin: NWS Flood Safety and Ready.gov Floods; new manuscript

action.text: If floodwater is rising around a vehicle, call 911 as soon as you can without delaying immediate escape from a sinking vehicle. Give the location, occupants and water conditions.

If safe high ground is immediately accessible without entering moving water, move to it. Otherwise tell dispatch what exits and hazards you can see and follow rescue instructions. A stalled vehicle in fast current is a specialist-rescue situation.
Never enter floodwater to follow another vehicle or save property. Do not depend on window glass type, vehicle stability or a predicted water depth.

failure.text: Sitting inside a stalled sedan in a flooded underpass calling roadside assistance until rising water pins the doors shut and shorts power windows.

verify.text: Confirm the group knows the turnaround rule and how to report a trapped vehicle without entering the water as a bystander.

stop.text: Rising or fast-moving water, structural uncertainty or a submerged route requires immediate emergency help.

title: Prepare low-lying homes proactively before spring snowmelt flood crests
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Floods and MN HSEM; new manuscript

action.text: Move vital documents, irreplaceable photos, medications, electronics, and hazardous basement chemicals (paints, fuels, pesticides—so floodwaters do NOT turn into toxic chemical soup!) up to upper floors well before flood crests arrive.

Test sump pumps and battery backups, clear storm drains/gutters safely, elevate or unplug lower-level appliances if dry, and follow official municipal guidance on sandbagging or utility shutoffs ONLY while access roads remain completely dry and open.
Park vehicles on verified high dry ground ahead of crest and evacuate early if authorities issue voluntary or mandatory flood evacuation orders.

failure.text: Leaving 5-gallon gas cans, lawn pesticides, and vital home deeds on a basement shelf until floodwater lifts them and contaminates the entire house.

verify.text: Confirm basement chemicals/valuables moved high, sump pump checked, cars parked high, and early departure timed before roads flood.

stop.text: Rising water entering the basement or approaching exit roads halts all home-prep tasks immediately—evacuate safely to high ground.

title: Avoid hidden biological, chemical, and electrical hazards in floodwater
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Floods and CDC Water; new manuscript

action.text: Treat EVERY drop of urban or rural floodwater as dangerous mixed hazard water containing **raw municipal/septic sewage, spilled heating oil/gasoline, agricultural pesticides, sharp submerged glass/metal, displaced wildlife, and potentially energized downed electrical lines**.

Keep children and pets completely OUT of flooded yards, ditches, and storm-drain puddles—never allow playing, wading, or kayaking in neighborhood floodwaters where submerged open storm culverts create deadly underwater suction traps.

If accidental skin contact occurs, wash immediately and thoroughly with soap and confirmed safe potable water, keep any open cuts covered cleanly, and seek prompt medical evaluation for any floodwater-exposed wound or tetanus update.

objective: Prevent electrocution, severe wound infections, chemical burns, and unseen drop-off drownings during and after floods.

verify.text: Confirm zero recreational wading, zero bare-skin floodwater contact, immediate soap/safe-water washing if splashed, and cuts escalated clinically.

stop.text: Downed wires near floodwater, fuel sheens, fast current, or open wounds prohibit entering the water completely.

title: Follow strict structural, utility, and mold clearance before post-flood re-entry
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Floods and EPA; new manuscript

action.text: Return ONLY after local officials declare the area safe, enter in **DAYLIGHT** using flashlights (zero matches/lighters), inspect exterior walls/foundation/porches for tilting, washed-out soil, or sagging ceilings BEFORE stepping inside, and exit immediately if you smell gas or hear hissing.

Keep main electricity OFF until a licensed electrician/utility verifies wet panels, outlets, and submerged appliances are safe, do NOT drink municipal tap or private well water until utility/certified-lab clearance issues, and photograph all damage thoroughly for insurance/FEMA BEFORE stripping debris.

Remove soaked drywall, insulation, carpet padding, and porous furniture cleanly wearing N95/gloves/goggles to halt rapid 24-to-48-hour mold growth, and NEVER run fuel-powered generators or dewatering pumps inside wet basements or garages.

title: Execute Ready-Set-Go wildfire evacuation tiers before smoke traps roads
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Wildfires; new manuscript

action.text: Learn the evacuation terms your locality uses before fire season. Stage documents, medications, pets and an accessible route early. Leave promptly when directed, using official routes.

Remember that wind shifts and spotting embers jump highways and change fire direction in minutes—if you feel unsafe or see thick advancing smoke/ash even BEFORE a formal Go order arrives, leave early on your own initiative.

Never stay behind trying to defend a house with a garden hose when mandatory evacuation orders issue—wildland fire storms overwhelm municipal water pressure and trap stay-behind residents behind burning trees.

title: Drive safely through wildfire evacuation corridors and avoid trap roads
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Wildfires and Evacuation; new manuscript

action.text: Leave early using official open routes. Follow responders’ guidance if smoke cuts visibility. Closed windows and recirculation may reduce particles briefly, but they do not make a vehicle safe in smoke, fire or carbon monoxide.

Do NOT follow smartphone GPS "shortcut" detours onto narrow gravel forest roads or dead-end side streets—apps routinely route evacuees straight into active fire flanks or locked logging gates; obey live deputies, fire crews, and official DOT closures.

Once clear of the fire perimeter, check in with your out-of-area relay contact and official evacuation shelter registry, and NEVER attempt to drive back inside fire lines until authorities formally lift closures.

title: Use live AirNow AQI categories to protect lungs from regional wildfire smoke
origin: US EPA AirNow Wildfires; new manuscript

action.text: Check live official **AirNow AQI** (PM2.5) readings rather than relying only on haze appearance: **Moderate (51–100)** alerts unusually sensitive groups; **Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups (101–150)** moves children, older adults, pregnant individuals, and people with asthma/heart/lung disease indoors; **Unhealthy (151–200)** and **Very Unhealthy / Hazardous (201+)** require EVERYONE to move indoors, close windows, and cancel heavy outdoor exertion.
Cut heavy outdoor running, yard work, and sports immediately as AQI climbs—strenuous breathing pulls deep fine PM2.5 particles far deeper into lung alveoli and bloodstream than quiet indoor rest.
Keep windows, doors, and fresh-air HVAC intakes tightly closed during high-AQI plumes, switching immediately to indoor clean-room filtration and keeping personal prescribed rescue inhalers at hand.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Scale outdoor exertion, indoor filtration, and vulnerable-person protections objectively using official PM2.5 Air Quality Index readings.
applies: Local wildfires AND long-range Canadian/western smoke plumes routinely blanketing Minnesota and the Upper Midwest.
equipment: Official AirNow.gov / local air-quality alerts, indoor clean-room HEPA purifier, and own prescribed asthma/heart inhalers.

failure.text: Holding outdoor youth soccer practice or heavy wood-splitting in Purple "Very Unhealthy" (AQI 230) smoke haze because "the fire is 500 miles away."

verify.text: Confirm official AirNow AQI checked, outdoor exertion scaled back/cancelled at thresholds, windows shut, and vulnerable members monitored.

stop.text: Wheezing, persistent cough, chest tightness, shortness of breath, or dizziness during smoke events requires clean indoor air immediately and 911/clinical evaluation.

title: Assemble and run an indoor HEPA clean room during prolonged wildfire smoke
origin: US EPA Create a Clean Room; new manuscript

action.text: Pick one comfortable interior room (often a bedroom) with minimal exterior doors/windows, close all exterior openings tightly, and run a **correctly sized portable HEPA air cleaner** continuously on high/medium—NEVER use an "ozone generator" or unverified ionizer air cleaner, which emits lung-damaging ozone gas!

If your home has central HVAC, set the system to **RECIRCULATE** (closing any fresh outdoor-air intake damper) and install a high-efficiency **MERV-13** (or highest rating your exact furnace blower safely supports per manual) filter replaced promptly when gray with smoke soot.

Eliminate ALL indoor particulate sources inside the clean room and house: NO frying/broiling on stoves, NO candles/incense, NO smoking/vaping, NO fireplaces, and NO vacuuming unless using a true sealed HEPA vacuum (regular vacuums stir fine settled ash back into breathing air).

objective: Create one low-particulate safe breathing room inside an ordinary home during multi-day smoke plumes without introducing indoor pollution or ozone.
applies: Multi-day Unhealthy/Hazardous wildfire smoke events impacting homes and apartments.
equipment: Correctly sized portable HEPA air cleaner (non-ozone-generating) OR compatible HVAC MERV-13 filter on recirculate, plus interior room with few openings.

failure.text: Running a portable HEPA purifier in the bedroom while frying bacon on a gas stove and burning scented candles in the kitchen next door.

verify.text: Confirm true non-ozone HEPA purifier sized to room square footage, HVAC on recirculate, windows closed, and zero indoor smoke/candle/frying sources.

stop.text: Indoor room temperatures climbing to unsafe heat-wave levels inside a sealed clean room require prioritizing heat-stroke safety via air-conditioned clean-air shelters.

title: Resolve compound smoke-plus-extreme-heat emergencies safely
origin: US EPA Clean Room and Ready.gov Heat; new manuscript

action.text: Closed windows may reduce smoke exposure while indoor heat increases. Check both conditions and look for cooled, cleaner-air shelter before a power or cooling failure occurs.

If your home lacks air conditioning (or power fails) during simultaneous smoke and extreme heat, relocate proactively to a public air-conditioned clean-air cooling center, library, mall, or cooled relative's home—taking vulnerable elders, infants, and asthmatics early.
Use recirculation when available and compatible with the cooling equipment. If the dwelling cannot stay cool and cleaner than outside, relocate when safe and follow local alerts.

title: Respect NIOSH N95/P100 particulate respirator limits in wildfire smoke
origin: US EPA AirNow Wildfires; new manuscript

action.text: Verify the respirator is stamped **NIOSH N95 or P100** with dual head straps (not loose single-loop dust masks, surgical masks, cloth gaiters, or bandanas, which leak fine PM2.5 smoke freely around the cheeks and nose).

Seal the nose clip and dual straps cleanly against smooth skin (heavy facial hair breaks the seal sharply, and standard adult N95s do NOT fit young children—keep children indoors in clean HEPA air instead).

Remember critical respirator boundaries: an N95/P100 filters solid fine smoke particles ONLY—it offers **ZERO protection against carbon monoxide, toxic chemical vapors, or oxygen-deficient air near active flames**; individuals with heart or lung disease should ask their clinician before prolonged respirator use.

title: Follow strict post-wildfire return clearance for ash pits, snags, and debris flows
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Wildfires and Landslides; new manuscript

action.text: Return ONLY after fire officials lift evacuation closures; walk carefully wearing thick leather boots, gloves, and N95 masks because gray ash heaps conceal **smoldering underground root embers and hot ash pits** capable of melting soles and causing deep burns weeks after flames pass.

Watch overhead constantly for silent falling fire-weakened trees ("snags"), burned wooden utility poles, damaged propane tanks, and downed power lines—and NEVER wet down deep toxic structural ash indiscriminately without PPE and local hazmat/debris guidance.

Stay alert for **years after a wildfire** during heavy rainstorms: burned hillsides lose root-soil stability and shed rain violently into fast-moving **flash floods and deadly debris flows** even from modest downpours.

title: Act early on Excessive Heat Warnings and high overnight low temperatures
origin: NWS Heat Safety and FEMA Extreme Heat; new manuscript

action.text: Monitor both daytime **Heat Index** (temperature + humidity) AND **overnight minimum temperatures**—when nighttime air stays above 75–80°F in un-air-conditioned homes, bodies never shed stored daytime heat, causing cumulative organ stress across days 2 through 5 of a heat wave.

Reschedule outdoor work, athletics, and errands strictly to early morning before peak sun, draw shades/blinds on sun-facing windows early, avoid running home ovens, wear light loose breathable clothes, and hydrate steadily with safe water before thirst lags.
Check TWICE DAILY on older adults, infants, pregnant individuals, outdoor workers, and neighbors taking heat-sensitive medications (such as diuretics or certain psychiatric/heart drugs).

title: Manage home cooling and follow the CDC indoor fan limit
origin: FEMA Extreme Heat and CDC Heat Health; new manuscript

action.text: CDC recommends fans only when indoor temperatures are below 90°F (32°C). In hotter rooms, use a cooler location or air conditioning rather than relying on a fan for protection.
Choose the coolest safe location and use cool showers or wet cloths if available. Avoid a basement if flood, gas or utility hazards make it unsafe.

Preserve grid stability safely when utilities issue conservation appeals only within safe indoor temperatures—never turn AC off for frail, elderly, or heat-vulnerable household members during Excessive Heat Warnings.

title: Prevent fatal parked-vehicle heat deaths with zero-exception look-before-locking rules
origin: FEMA Extreme Heat and NPS Desert Safety; new manuscript

action.text: NEVER leave a child, dependent adult, or pet alone inside a parked vehicle for even **"just two minutes"**—greenhouse solar heating spikes cabin temperatures by roughly 20°F in 10 minutes and can reach fatal temperatures above 120°F even when outdoor air is a mild 70°F and windows are cracked open.

Build automatic fail-safe habits to defeat routine-change memory slips: place your purse, work badge, lunch bag, or left shoe right beside the rear child car seat, ALWAYS open the back door to look before locking, and keep parked cars locked at home so toddlers cannot climb inside unattended.

If you ever see a child or pet locked alone in a hot parked car showing distress or unresponsiveness, call **911 IMMEDIATELY** and follow dispatcher/Good Samaritan legal guidance to get them out and begin immediate rapid cooling.

title: Locate public cooling centers early and run twice-daily neighbor heat checks

Plan spending the hottest peak hours (roughly 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.) inside air-conditioned spaces whenever home cooling fails—just several continuous hours in cool AC dramatically lowers cumulative cardiovascular and kidney strain.

Check in by phone or brief daytime door knock at least TWICE DAILY on older neighbors, people living alone, and households without AC—summoning 911 promptly if someone fails to answer or appears flushed, confused, or dizzy.

title: Coordinate immediate rapid cooling and 911 for community heat-stroke collapse
origin: CDC NIOSH Heat Illnesses and Ready.gov Heat; new manuscript

action.text: Treat ANY sudden confusion, slurred speech, stumbling, agitation, seizure, fainting, or hot skin during a heat wave as **LIFE-THREATENING HEAT STROKE**—call **911 IMMEDIATELY** and move the person into shade or air conditioning without delay.

Start cooling while help is on the way. Move to shade or a cooler place when safe and cool the skin with water and airflow. Discuss immersion with dispatch, particularly when airway protection, patient type or available help is uncertain.
Give nothing by mouth to a confused or drowsy person. Monitor breathing and follow 911 instructions until EMS arrives.

title: Anticipate cascading infrastructure failures during prolonged grid blackouts
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Power Outages; new manuscript

action.text: Map the cascading chain BEFORE storms hit: when regional power drops, **gas-station fuel pumps stop**, **ATMs and credit-card terminals go offline**, **cell-tower backup batteries drain within hours to a day**, **elevators and residential well/septic pumps stop**, and **municipal water pressure may drop** triggering Boil Water notices.

Build simple everyday habits that buffer cascading failures automatically: keep vehicle fuel above **HALF-TANK** year-round, maintain small-denomination cash, keep stored potable water and FIFO pantry food ready, and store critical phone numbers and medication lists on paper.

Understand utility restoration order realistically: crews clear life-threatening downed wires first, then restore high-voltage transmission lines, substations, hospitals/water plants, main feeders, and finally isolated residential tap lines—so individual rural or side-street homes can wait days longer than downtown corridors.

title: Manage multi-day electrical outages safely without indoor combustion or fires
origin: FEMA Power Outages and CPSC; new manuscript

action.text: Establish a calm daily blackout rhythm right away: switch to low-mode LED lighting (zero candles), log power-off times and guard refrigerator/freezer doors, unplug surge-sensitive electronics/heaters, and conserve smartphone power strictly for brief SMS check-ins and 911.

Enforce ZERO indoor combustion compromises across every day of the outage—keep portable generators ≥20 feet outdoors with exhaust away from structures, cook strictly outdoors on grills/camp stoves (or eat no-cook pantry meals), and never heat homes with gas ovens or charcoal.
Track household health, indoor room temperature, water supply, and fuel/battery burn rate daily so you relocate cleanly to powered shelter or community hubs BEFORE reserves hit zero.

Follow the active advisory for icemakers, brushing teeth, preparing food and infant feeding. Use an approved alternative supply when required. Boiling is an option only for a microbial advisory and only as directed.
Wait for the local authority to lift the advisory and follow its flushing, appliance and filter directions.

Monitor county radio/211 for official municipal bulk-water tanker or bottled-water distribution sites, bringing clean, sanitized, clearly labeled **DRINKING WATER** food-grade containers (never dirty utility buckets or old chemical jugs) to refill early before home stocks run dry.

title: Adapt cleanly when cellular networks congest, broadband drops, and 911 is degraded

Note that Text-to-911 availability varies by county (call voice 911 first whenever possible; use Text-to-911 only where supported or if unable to speak)—and if ALL phone networks fail completely during a life-threatening emergency, know the physical address of your nearest staffed fire station, police precinct, or hospital.

Keep small-denomination physical cash ($1s, $5s, $10s, $20s) stored securely alongside vital documents so you can purchase food, ice, lodging, or fuel at generator-backed rural stores when broadband card terminals and ATMs stay dark.
Never hoard gasoline in unapproved jugs, glass bottles, or inside car trunks/living quarters during storm panics—spilled fuel vapors ignite explosively from static sparks or rear-end collisions.

title: Shelter-in-place properly for chemical or hazardous-materials airborne plumes
origin: FEMA Ready.gov Hazardous Materials Incidents; new manuscript

action.text: When local officials direct chemical shelter-in-place, go indoors and follow their directions for windows, doors and shutting off outside-air systems. Keep an alert channel active.

Use the interior room and temporary sealing measures specified by authorities. Room location depends on the release, building and local instructions. Do not infer a safe floor from the chemical name or odor.

Stay alert for changes. Follow official all-clear instructions on when to leave, ventilate or evacuate. A gas leak or carbon monoxide alarm inside the dwelling calls for getting out and calling 911 from safety.

action.text: For wildfire particles use cleaner indoor air and filtered recirculation if the building can stay cool. Relocate early if it cannot. For an external chemical release follow specific directions on room and ventilation controls.
HEPA filters remove particles. They do not make a room safe from all chemicals or carbon monoxide. Follow emergency directions rather than substituting one shelter method for another.
Always follow live local fire, hazmat, and emergency-management directives first—never apply a wildfire smoke guide to a chemical tanker spill or an indoor CO alarm.

title: Decide objectively between shelter-in-place and evacuation by hazard and official order

action.text: **EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY** whenever authorities issue a mandatory evacuation order, flames/floodwater threaten routes, indoor gas/CO/structural hazards occur, or prolonged utility loss pushes indoor heat/cold/medical batteries past safe floors while roads remain open.

**SHELTER IN PLACE** when moving outside exposes occupants to greater immediate danger than staying inside—such as active Tornado Warnings, lightning/derecho squalls, blinding whiteout blizzards, impassable flash floods, or official short-term hazmat Shelter-in-Place orders.

Re-evaluate continuously as conditions evolve: a safe blizzard shelter-in-place on Day 1 can shift into a necessary daylight warming-center evacuation on Day 3 once roads plow open and indoor temperatures fall.

Drive both routes once in daylight during calm weather so every household driver recognizes intersections, low-lying flood bridges to avoid, and rural gravel dead-ends.

During an active disaster evacuation, **FOLLOW LIVE LAW-ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS, FIRE CREWS, AND OFFICIAL DOT ROAD CLOSURES—NOT SMARTPHONE GPS SHORTCUTS**, because crowdsourced traffic apps automatically divert drivers off congested main highways onto flooded side roads, downed-wire streets, or burning flanks.

Run a verbal headcount at THREE fixed checkpoints: 1) before leaving the building, 2) inside the vehicle or at the neighborhood rally point, and 3) upon arriving at the shelter or out-of-town rally point—immediately texting status to your out-of-area relay contact.

Know exact school and daycare emergency reunification rules (official photo ID required, pre-listed backup authorized adults, designated off-site reunification center)—never rush an active emergency perimeter without following official reunification instructions.

Bring personal medications, hearing/mobility aids, infant formula/diapers, pillow/blanket, phone chargers, and earplugs—remember general public shelters prohibit weapons, alcohol, illegal drugs, and personal cooking flames indoors.

Understand the exact legal distinction for animals: **ADA-defined trained service animals** are legally admitted inside general public emergency shelters with their handler, whereas **companion pets** typically require designated pet-friendly shelters or co-located animal-shelter bays—verify county pet-shelter sites BEFORE storms hit!

title: Evacuate companion animals and prepare rural livestock contingencies safely

title: Phase a 30-day regional disruption into stabilization, adaptation, and recovery

Shift purposefully into **Days 4–14 (Adapt):** Establish daily water/food/battery pacing logs, reliable sanitation and hygiene stations, neighborhood wellness check-ins, and safe resupply trips to county distribution hubs or open towns.

Transition cleanly into **Days 15–30 (Sustain & Recover):** Maintain health/morale routines, monitor reserve replenishment triggers with 48-hour buffers, coordinate mutual aid and county/FEMA assistance claims, and execute safe phased utility restoration as infrastructure returns.

title: Run daily household water, food, fuel, and battery pacing logs over 30 days
origin: FEMA Ready.gov and CDC Emergency Water; new manuscript

action.text: Spend five calm minutes every evening writing down FOUR concrete numbers on paper: **potable drinking-water gallons left**, **days of familiar pantry food left**, **heating/generator/vehicle fuel left**, and **battery/medical-power charge state** (plus prescription days remaining).

Eat household food in smart spoilage order across weeks: **1)** Safe-temp refrigerated perishables first, **2)** Safe frozen items if power fails, **3)** Root-cellar/fresh produce showing early age, and **4)** Rotated shelf-stable canned and dry pantry staples last.

title: Sustain household hygiene, laundry, waste, and illness isolation across 30 days

Rotate demanding watch duties (storm monitoring, stove/wood tending, caregiver shifts) fairly so no single adult collapses from 72 hours without sleep and makes dangerous safety mistakes (like mis-placing a generator or forgetting a valve).
